# Part 1: Matrices

1\. Generate two matrices, `A` and `B`, containing randomly generated and normally distributed numbers. The dimensions of these two matrices should be $4 \times 3$ and $3 \times 6$, respectively. Confirm that `C <- A %*% B` produces the same results as:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
m <- nrow(A)
p <- ncol(B)
AB <- matrix(0, m, p)
for(i in 1:m){
  for(j in 1:p){
    AB[i,j] <- sum(A[i,] * B[,j])
  }
}
```

2\. Solve the following system of equations using R:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x + y + z + w &= 10\\
2x + 3y - z - w &= 5\\
3x - y + 4z - 2w &= 15\\
2x + 2y - 2z - 2w &= 20\\ 
\end{aligned}
$$

3\. Define `x` and `y`:

```{r}
#| eval: false

mnist <- read_mnist()
x <- mnist$train$images[1:300,] 
y <- mnist$train$labels[1:300]
```

and compute the distance matrix:

```{r}
#| eval: false

d <- dist(x)
class(d)
```

Generate a boxplot showing the distances from the second row of `d` to all other observations, stratified by digit label. Do not include the distance to itself, which we know is a distance of 0. Based on the boxplot, can you predict what digit is represented by the second row of `x`?

4\. Use the `apply` function and matrix algebra to compute the distance between the fourth digit `mnist$train$images[4,]` and all other digits represented in `mnist$train$images`. Then generate a boxplot as in exercise 3 and predict what digit is in the fourth row.

6\.  Based on the image views of rotations (third graphic in [this section](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/highdim/dimension-reduction.html#mnist-example)), which digit is most likely to be well-isolated
by PC1?  Provide the code that presents the boxplots for values of PC1 stratified by digit label to demonstrate this.

7\.  Provide the code that expands the image displays of rotation matrices for PC5-PC8.

8\.  Consider this code:
```
npcs = predict(pca, newdata=mnist$test$images)
tem = lm(npcs[,2]~factor(mnist$test$labels)-1)
plot(0:9, coef(tem))
```
Explain why this is in some ways a better way of looking at
the effectiveness of a computed principal component as
a discriminator of classes of inputs.
